messages.content: Analyze this sentence.  "Consydre thou myne condicyon; reflecte upon myne fader. Shall I forsake hym, when he is strycken wyth blyndnesse and destytute, to wrastle wyth infirmitie and penurye, when it lyeth wythin my poure to rendre hys latter yeeres fylled wyth comforte and joye?" Each paragraph of your response must end with the same word it started with, separate paragraphs with a newline.

message.content:
Consider the structure of this sentence: it opens with two imperatives—"Consydre thou myne condicyon; reflecte upon myne fader"—before pivoting into a sweeping rhetorical question about filial obligation, and the pivot works because the commands set the tone of solemn self-examination that the question then releases, forcing the listener to consider.

Rhetorical devices abound throughout: the direct address "thou" personalizes the plea, the semicolon links two parallel imperatives, the cascading image of "blyndnesse and destytute" followed by "infirmitie and penurye" builds an escalating portrait of decline, and the final contrast between the father's suffering and the speaker's stated capacity to alleviate it turns the whole passage into an indictment of inaction, making the structure itself rhetorical.

Duty is the moral engine of this sentence: the speaker frames filial care not as optional charity but as a natural, inescapable obligation, and the rhetorical question "Shall I forsake hym?" implies that the answer is so obviously no that merely posing the question becomes a moral test, binding the hearer to the duty.

Power is the pivot of the final clause: the speaker acknowledges that "it lyeth wythin my poure to rendre hys latter yeeres fylled wyth comforte and joye," and this admission transforms the earlier image of the father's helplessness into an indictment of potential inaction, because if the power to help exists, then the failure to use it becomes a conscious moral choice, and the burden of that power.

Joy is the final, almost unexpected word in this somber passage: after blindness, destitution, infirmity, and penury, the sentence closes not with a warning or a curse but with the possibility of "comforte and joye," and this closing brightness is what makes the rhetorical question so devastating, because the speaker is not merely asking whether he can endure his own burden but whether he can deny his father the very joy.
